books.title: 2025 accounts
books.source: From the 2025 consolidated financial statements, as compiled in the Canadian Labour Congress report, pp. 24–25.

article.author: The Data Desk
article.recordLede: The projection rests on what happened elsewhere. The record covers five countries and three decades; one academic study shows genuine benefits alongside the bill.
article.sourcesLede: The reporting carries a footnote block of 15 sources and a closing list of 20. Both are shown.
article.footer: Every paragraph above comes from the reporting; the projections are anchored to its figures and labelled as modelled.
article.seeYear: See this year on the board

sources.listedOnly: listed, not cited in the text
sources.anchors: Reported anchors: Perth +60 percent per passenger over a decade, UK parking at £98 a day, a 15–20 percent investor requirement, and a 40 percent workforce cut at Sydney.

figures.tripTitle: The fare barely moves. Everything around it does.
figures.tripDeck: Your {{ticket}} fare at {{code}} becomes a {{total}} trip by {{calendar}}. The green line is the ticket; the red line is everything you pay between the kerb and the gate.
figures.tripSource: Green: airfare, Improvement Fee, aeronautical charges and taxes. Red adds parking, drop-off, food and retail. Aeronautical charges rise at the rate that reproduces Perth’s reported +60 percent per passenger over a decade; non-ticket charges reach the levels documented in the UK.
figures.ticketTitle: Your ticket against your whole trip
figures.ticketEmpty: Answer the two questions above to see this chart drawn with your airport and your fare.
figures.insideDeck: Reported figures, not projections: the Improvement Fee is charged per departing passenger and makes up about a third of large-airport revenue. Taxes and fees are 25–35 percent of a Canadian ticket and are set at 28 percent here.
figures.insideSource: Improvement Fee and revenue shares from the 2025 statements; tax and fee share and the affordability ranking from the Canadian Labour Congress.

workforce.title: Cuts at Sydney’s rate would remove about 3,400 jobs from the four airports
workforce.deck: Sydney’s new owners cut 40 percent of the workforce once post-sale protections expired. Applied to the airports in scope at typical staffing density, that is the scale of the exposure.
workforce.source: Staffing modelled at 62 jobs per million annual passengers. The 40 percent cut is the figure reported for Sydney Airport.
workforce.legendCut: in scope for a Sydney-scale cut

figures.journeyTitle: The charges, in the order you meet them
figures.journeyDeck: Privatisation does not raise one price. It raises a series of small ones, each of which is defensible on its own.
figures.journeySource: Drop-off and parking levels from the UK evidence; the safety warning from the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.
figures.revenueTitle: A one-time windfall against a permanent extraction
figures.revenueDeck: Airport authorities made no profit at all off the $3.95 billion they took in during 2022 — expenses and revenues were effectively identical. A private operator has to do the opposite.
figures.revenueSource: Revenue base and the $525 million annual rent from the reporting. The 15–20 percent investor return is the Canadian Labour Congress estimate; the 37 percent Improvement Fee share is the CCPA’s.

revenue.publicBodyA: Revenue in 2022. Surpluses go back into the airports, and about
revenue.publicBodyB: returns to the federal government as rent.
revenue.privateBodyA: Extra revenue needed every year, at 17.5 percent of revenue — the midpoint of the 15–20 percent band. That is
revenue.privateBodyB: a year, every year, found from airlines, retailers or passengers.

figures.serviceTitle: The study that cuts both ways
figures.serviceDeck: A 2023 University of Alberta study is the strongest evidence in the article for privatisation. It found real improvements — and it found the bill.
figures.serviceSource: University of Alberta study as reported, and the Canadian Labour Congress review.
figures.serviceImprovedBody: Flight cancellations under private equity ownership, alongside higher customer satisfaction and better terminals.
figures.serviceCostBody: More in fees per passenger, confirmed by the same research. The study did not show one effect without the other.
figures.serviceAccc: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission put the risk plainly: under price-cap regulation there may be incentives to increase profits by reducing costs, and “in some cases such cost cutting may lead to a lower quality of service.” The commission built service-quality monitoring specifically to detect it.
figures.lockTitle: A contract longer than most careers, mortgages and governments
figures.lockDeck: The concessions described run 50 to 99 years. Once signed, buying the contract back is prohibitively expensive.
figures.lockSource: Concession length and the P3 warning from the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.
figures.evidenceDeck: A consistent pattern across Australia, New Zealand, Portugal, the United Kingdom and the United States: higher charges, pressure on workers and the loss of long-term public value.
figures.promisesDeck: Of the {{total}} claims made for the deal, {{atRisk}} with a documented failure mode in the record, {{unproven}} unproven, and {{supported}} backed by evidence.
figures.promisesSource: Statuses are this article’s judgement, drawn from what the reporting shows about the same claims in Australia, the United Kingdom and Brazil.

detail.dropFree: {{code}} allows {{free}} free minutes, so your {{minutes}}-minute stop is free. British airports charge up to $24 for the same stop.
detail.dropPaid: {{minutes}} minutes at the kerb exceeds the {{free}} free minutes {{code}} allows today. British airports charge up to $24 for exactly this.
detail.securityBody: The charge that never appears on a receipt. The CCPA warns that cutting staff and staff pay “isn’t only about comfort in an airport, it can also be about traveller safety.”
detail.foodBody: Rents rise, so the sandwich does. Modelled from 6 percent of your ticket today to the 19 percent share UK travellers pay once retail is optimised for profit.
detail.parkingBody: {{price}} a day at {{code}} today, moving toward Heathrow-scale pricing of $59 a day. Five English airports collected £751 million in parking fees in 2025 alone.
